newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists offer elections a year early.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists offer elections a year early.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists, buffeted by nine days of street protests, appeared on Wednesday to soften their stand on opposition calls for a general election and suggested an early poll before the end of this year.
The party's opponents have organised the protests on the back of public anger over deepening economic hardship and workers held a series of one-hour warning strikes around the country on Wednesday.
A poll before end-1997 would be a year ahead of schedule.

"We are prepared to hold elections by the end of the year and negotiations should start here and now," Krassimir Premyanov, head of the Socialist's parliamentary group, told the legislature, which reopened after coming under siege and being ransacked by opposition protesters last Friday.

A spokesman for the main opposition trade union Podkrepa said coal miners, steel workers and staff at weapons plants in the town of Sopot took strike action early on Wednesday and he expected more protests during the day.
Port workers in Varna stopped work for an hour, and taxis planned to block roads in several cities.
By law, full-blown strikes require a week's notice.

The opposition is boycotting parliament until its demands for an election are met, but 123 deputies from the Socialist Party, the Bulgarian Business Bloc and smaller parties attended the session, which had an agenda of routine business.

The building, repaired and cleared of debris, was surrounded by riot police who have cordoned it off since protesters attacked on Friday after the Socialists refused to vote on an opposition motion calling for early elections.
On Tuesday, the Socialists' parliamentary group said it wanted to form a new government to implement a 500-day programme, which would take it close to the end of its mandate.
The opposition Union of Democratic Forces leader, Ivan Kostov, said the coalition was meeting on Wednesday morning. He had no immediate reaction to the latest apparent concession.

Nikolai Kamov, a leading member of the divided Socialist party's reformist wing, said the leadership's decision did not go far enough. He said the only solution was to dissolve parliament, adding that many deputies privately agreed with him.
"When your opponent refuses negotiations and demands are dictated by powerful waves of protests, the cleanest solution is to agree to their demands and dissolve parliament," he said.
Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov was meeting President Zhelyu Zhelev, who has refused to ask the Socialists to form a government.
The Bulgarian Business Bloc, Bulgaria's third political force, said it had withdrawn parliamentary support for the embattled ruling party.

A Socialist party spokeswoman said party leaders had agreed at a meeting on Tuesday that they should form an interim government of "professionals with experience and international authority" to govern until the elections.
Year-on-year inflation is currently running at a rate of more than 300 percent and living standards have plunged since the ex-communist Socialist party came to power in a general election in 1994.

The party's failure to introduce market reforms and its powerful allies in business are being blamed for a flight of capital that has helped push the lev down to nearly 700 to the dollar from 70 a year ago. This has resulted in most salaries being degraded to the point where they are worth the equivalent of only a few dollars a month.
The World Bank said on Tuesday it was extremely worried about the economy and urged the implementation of a stalled programme of privatisation and other reforms.
Quick formation of a new cabinet is seen as vital to secure a new funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
